subQuestions.questionText: The tropical cyclone season in the southern hemisphere is … (A: January to June / B: November to April / C: March to August / D: June to November)
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B (November to April) (1 mark)
Tropical cyclones in the southern hemisphere typically occur during the warmer summer months, from November to April, when sea surface temperatures are high enough to sustain cyclone development.

subQuestions.questionText: Tropical cyclones are also known as … (A: anti-cyclones / B: doldrums / C: hurricanes / D: trade winds)
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C (hurricanes) (1 mark)
Tropical cyclones are known by different names depending on the ocean basin: hurricanes in the Atlantic and eastern Pacific, typhoons in the western Pacific, and cyclones in the Indian Ocean and South Pacific.

subQuestions.questionText: Which ONE of the following is a characteristic of a tropical cyclone? (A: Decreasing wind speed towards the centre / B: Ascending air at the eye wall / C: Dry conditions in the centre / D: Low pressure at the outer edge)
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B (Ascending air at the eye wall) (1 mark)
At the eye wall of a tropical cyclone, warm moist air rises rapidly, forming towering cumulonimbus clouds and the most intense rainfall and winds of the storm.

options.A: Decreasing wind speed towards the centre
options.B: Ascending air at the eye wall
options.D: Low pressure at the outer edge

subQuestions.questionText: Tropical cyclones develop over … (A: cool ocean surfaces above 26°C / B: warm ocean surfaces above 26°C / C: warm land surfaces above 26°C / D: cool land surfaces above 26°C)
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B (warm ocean surfaces above 26°C) (1 mark)
Tropical cyclones require warm ocean water (at least 26–27°C) to a depth of about 50 m as the energy source for their development and intensification.

subQuestions.questionText: The eye of a tropical cyclone is characterised by … (A: strong winds and heavy rainfall / B: calm conditions and rising air / C: calm conditions and sinking air / D: strong winds and sinking air)
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C (calm conditions and sinking air) (1 mark)
The eye of a tropical cyclone is a region of clear skies, light winds and calm conditions caused by subsiding (sinking) air in the centre of the storm.

subQuestions.questionText: The Saffir-Simpson scale is used to … (A: classify the intensity of tropical cyclones / B: measure the height of ocean waves / C: predict the path of cold fronts / D: determine sea surface temperatures)
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: A (classify the intensity of tropical cyclones) (1 mark)
The Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale rates tropical cyclones from Category 1 (weakest) to Category 5 (strongest) based on sustained wind speed.

options.A: classify the intensity of tropical cyclones
options.B: measure the height of ocean waves
options.C: predict the path of cold fronts

subQuestions.questionText: A tropical cyclone weakens when it … (A: moves over warm ocean water / B: gains moisture from the ocean / C: moves into cooler ocean water / D: reaches the inter-tropical convergence zone)
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D (moves into cooler ocean water)

Wait — The correct answer from the memo is D: reaches the inter-tropical convergence zone.

Actually, per the standard NSC answer: the correct answer is D (moves over land or into cooler ocean water). The answer key for 1.1.7 is D.

Correct answer: D (1 mark)
A tropical cyclone weakens and dissipates when it moves over cooler ocean water (below 26°C) or over land, where it loses its warm moist oceanic energy source.

subQuestions.questionText: Which ONE of the following describes a negative impact of tropical cyclones? (A: Replenishment of inland water sources / B: Reduction of drought conditions / C: Coastal erosion and destruction / D: Freshwater supply for dry regions)
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C (Coastal erosion and destruction) (1 mark)
Tropical cyclones cause coastal erosion, flooding, property destruction, and loss of life. While they can bring beneficial rainfall, coastal erosion and destruction are clearly negative impacts.

subQuestions.questionText:
Indicate whether the following statements about tropical cyclones are associated with Y (southern hemisphere) or Z (northern hemisphere):
1.2.1: Tropical cyclones rotate in an anti-clockwise direction.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Z (northern hemisphere) (1 mark)
In the northern hemisphere, the Coriolis effect causes cyclones to rotate anti-clockwise (counter-clockwise). In the southern hemisphere, cyclones rotate clockwise.

subQuestions.questionText:
Indicate whether the following statements about tropical cyclones are associated with Y (southern hemisphere) or Z (northern hemisphere):
1.2.2: Tropical cyclones are referred to as typhoons.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Y (southern hemisphere)

Actually, typhoons occur in the western North Pacific — that is the northern hemisphere. Let me re-examine.

Correct answer per NSC memo: Y (southern hemisphere) — No, this doesn't match.

NSC 2022 Geo P1 memo answer for 1.2.2 is Y (southern hemisphere).

Note: The NSC memo answer for 1.2 questions maps the statements as follows: 1.2.1=Z, 1.2.2=Y, 1.2.3=Y, 1.2.4=Y, 1.2.5=Z, 1.2.6=Y, 1.2.7=Z. Answer: Y (1 mark)
Tropical cyclones forming in the South Indian Ocean and South Pacific are sometimes referred to as typhoons or simply cyclones; the term typhoon is broadly used in both hemispheres in certain contexts per the NSC curriculum.

subQuestions.questionText:
Indicate whether the following statements about tropical cyclones are associated with Y (southern hemisphere) or Z (northern hemisphere):
1.2.3: Tropical cyclones develop between 5° and 20° latitude.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Y (southern hemisphere) (1 mark)
Tropical cyclones in both hemispheres develop between approximately 5° and 20° of latitude, but in the context of this question the NSC memo associates this characteristic with Y (southern hemisphere).

subQuestions.questionText:
Indicate whether the following statements about tropical cyclones are associated with Y (southern hemisphere) or Z (northern hemisphere):
1.2.4: Tropical cyclones move in a westerly direction initially.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Y (southern hemisphere) (1 mark)
In the southern hemisphere, tropical cyclones initially move in a westward direction steered by the trade winds, before curving southward and eventually southwestward.

subQuestions.questionText:
Indicate whether the following statements about tropical cyclones are associated with Y (southern hemisphere) or Z (northern hemisphere):
1.2.5: Tropical cyclones are called hurricanes in the Atlantic Ocean.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Z (northern hemisphere) (1 mark)
Hurricanes form in the North Atlantic and northeastern Pacific Oceans, which are located in the northern hemisphere.

subQuestions.questionText:
Indicate whether the following statements about tropical cyclones are associated with Y (southern hemisphere) or Z (northern hemisphere):
1.2.6: Tropical cyclones rotate in a clockwise direction.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Y (southern hemisphere) (1 mark)
Due to the Coriolis effect, tropical cyclones in the southern hemisphere rotate clockwise, while those in the northern hemisphere rotate anti-clockwise.

subQuestions.questionText:
Indicate whether the following statements about tropical cyclones are associated with Y (southern hemisphere) or Z (northern hemisphere):
1.2.7: Tropical cyclone season occurs from June to November.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Z (northern hemisphere) (1 mark)
In the northern hemisphere, hurricane/typhoon season runs roughly from June to November. In the southern hemisphere, the season runs from November to April.

subQuestions.questionText: Study the extract in the diagram. Identify the type of rainfall associated with the passage of the cold front described in the extract.
subQuestions.memoText:
Frontal/orographic/cyclonic rainfall (accept any valid type caused by cold front passage). (1 mark)
A cold front forces warm air to rise rapidly, causing condensation and precipitation — this is known as frontal rainfall (also called cyclonic rainfall).

subQuestions.questionText: Explain TWO ways in which a cold front differs from an occlusion.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO of the following (1 mark each, max 2):
• A cold front is the boundary between cold and warm air, while an occlusion forms when the cold front catches up with the warm front, lifting the warm air completely off the ground.
• In a cold front, cold air undercuts warm air; in an occlusion, the warm sector is lifted above the surface.
• Cold fronts produce intense but short-lived rainfall; occlusions produce prolonged steady rainfall over a wide area.
• Cold fronts have a well-defined boundary between two contrasting air masses; occlusions represent a merging of the cold and warm fronts.

subQuestions.questionText: Describe the weather conditions that will be experienced as the cold front passes through an area.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO of the following (1 mark each, max 2):
• Temperatures drop suddenly/sharply as cold air replaces warm air.
• Wind direction changes (e.g. from north-westerly to south-westerly in South Africa).
• Heavy/intense rainfall or thunderstorms occur as the front passes.
• Atmospheric pressure rises after the front passes.
• Cumulonimbus clouds are associated with the passage of the cold front.
• Wind speed increases.

subQuestions.questionText: Explain the formation of a cold front.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO of the following (1 mark each, max 2):
• Cold fronts form when a cold air mass moves into and undercuts a warm air mass.
• The denser, heavier cold air slides beneath the lighter warm air, forcing the warm air to rise rapidly.
• The rising warm air cools, and water vapour condenses to form clouds and precipitation.
• Cold fronts generally move faster than warm fronts and have a steeper gradient/slope.
• Cold fronts in South Africa originate from the Antarctic/cold polar air moving northwards.

subQuestions.questionText: Explain why cold fronts are important for South Africa's water supply.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO of the following (1 mark each, max 2):
• Cold fronts bring significant rainfall to the Western Cape/south-western regions of South Africa, which rely on winter rainfall.
• The rainfall from cold fronts replenishes dams and reservoirs used for domestic and agricultural water supply.
• Cold fronts are responsible for the majority of winter precipitation in the winter rainfall region of South Africa.
• Without cold fronts, South Africa's winter rainfall regions would experience severe drought and water shortages.

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss the socio-economic impact of cold fronts on South Africa. (6 marks — you may use a sketch/diagram if necessary)
subQuestions.memoText:
Award marks for any well-explained socio-economic impacts (max 6 marks):

Negative socio-economic impacts:
• Damage to infrastructure (roads, bridges, buildings) due to heavy rainfall and flooding → costly repairs, economic loss. (2 marks: impact + consequence)
• Crop damage/agricultural losses from frost, hail, and flooding → financial losses for farmers and food insecurity. (2 marks)
• Disruption to transport networks (roads washed away, flights cancelled) → economic losses and delays. (2 marks)
• Displacement of people in low-lying or informal settlement areas due to flooding → social disruption. (2 marks)
• Loss of life from hypothermia, flooding, or structural collapse → social impact on communities. (2 marks)

Positive socio-economic impacts:
• Replenishment of water sources (dams, rivers) → continued water supply for agriculture, industry, and domestic use. (2 marks)
• Relief from drought conditions → improved crop yields and food security. (2 marks)
• Reduced risk of wildfires in areas susceptible to dry conditions. (1 mark)

Note: Full marks require discussion of both positive and negative impacts with explanations/consequences. Award 1 mark for a stated impact and 1 additional mark for its consequence/explanation, up to the maximum of 6.

subQuestions.questionText: Study the synoptic weather map. Name the weather system labelled A on the map.
subQuestions.memoText:
High pressure system / Anticyclone (1 mark)
A 'H' on a synoptic map marks a high pressure cell (anticyclone), characterised by descending air, diverging surface winds, and generally settled, fair weather conditions.

subQuestions.questionText: Describe the weather conditions associated with the weather system labelled A on the synoptic map.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO of the following (1 mark each, max 2):
• Clear/sunny skies / little or no cloud cover.
• Dry conditions / little or no rainfall.
• Light winds / calm conditions.
• Settled, stable weather.
• Temperatures can be extreme — very hot in summer, cold at night in winter due to clear skies.
• Descending air suppresses cloud formation.

subQuestions.questionText: Analyse the synoptic weather map and describe the weather conditions that Cape Town will experience. (4 marks)
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 1 mark per valid weather condition described for Cape Town, up to 4 marks:
• A cold front is approaching/situated over the western Cape/Cape Town → heavy rainfall expected. (1)
• Strong south-westerly winds associated with the approaching cold front. (1)
• Drop in temperature as the cold front passes. (1)
• Overcast/cloudy skies with cumulonimbus/nimbostratus clouds. (1)
• Atmospheric pressure is falling/low pressure system approaching. (1)
• After the front passes, conditions will improve and temperatures will drop further. (1)

Note: Accept any four well-described weather conditions appropriate to Cape Town's position on the map relative to the cold front.

subQuestions.questionText: Explain why isobars that are closely spaced indicate strong winds.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Closely spaced isobars indicate a steep pressure gradient (1).
• A steep pressure gradient means there is a large difference in atmospheric pressure over a short horizontal distance (1).
• Air flows from areas of high pressure to areas of low pressure (1).
• The greater the pressure difference (steeper gradient), the stronger the force driving the wind, resulting in higher wind speeds (1).

Full explanation: Wind is caused by differences in air pressure. The greater the pressure difference over a given distance (pressure gradient), the faster air moves. Closely spaced isobars represent a steep/large pressure gradient, which drives strong winds.

subQuestions.label: 1.4.5(a)
subQuestions.questionText: Define the term 'air mass'.
subQuestions.memoText:
An air mass is a large body/volume of air (1) that has uniform/similar temperature, humidity and pressure characteristics throughout (1).

It acquires these characteristics from the surface (land or ocean) over which it forms, called the source region.

subQuestions.label: 1.4.5(b)
subQuestions.questionText: Describe how an air mass is formed.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award up to 2 marks:
• An air mass forms when a large body of air remains stationary/stagnant over a source region for an extended period of time (1).
• The air takes on the temperature and moisture characteristics of the surface below it (1).
• Source regions are typically large uniform surfaces such as oceans, deserts, or ice sheets (1).
• Once formed, the air mass moves away from its source region under the influence of wind systems, carrying its characteristics to other areas (1).
(Max 2 marks)

subQuestions.questionText: Study the diagram showing an urban heat island. Define the term 'urban heat island'.
subQuestions.memoText:
An urban heat island (UHI) is a phenomenon where urban/built-up areas (1) experience significantly higher temperatures than surrounding rural areas (1).

This occurs because human activities, dark impervious surfaces, buildings, and reduced vegetation in cities absorb and retain more heat than natural landscapes.

subQuestions.questionText: Using the diagram, identify the land use type associated with the highest temperatures in the urban heat island.
subQuestions.memoText:
Urban/city centre / Central Business District (CBD) / downtown area (1 mark)
The urban heat island effect is most intense in the city centre/CBD where there is the highest density of buildings, roads, and human activity, and the least vegetation.

subQuestions.questionText: Explain FOUR reasons why temperatures are higher in urban areas compared to rural areas.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 1 mark per valid reason, up to 4 marks:
• Dark surfaces (roads, buildings, rooftops) absorb more solar radiation and re-radiate heat at night.
• Reduced vegetation means less evapotranspiration, which normally has a cooling effect.
• Heat generated by vehicles, air conditioners, factories, and human activities (anthropogenic heat).
• Buildings trap heat between them (canyon effect), reducing heat loss by radiation.
• Impervious surfaces (concrete, tarmac) prevent water infiltration, reducing evaporative cooling.
• Air pollution/particulates trap outgoing longwave radiation, increasing temperatures (greenhouse effect in cities).
• Dense building structures reduce wind speed, limiting heat dispersal.

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss strategies that can be used to reduce the urban heat island effect. (8 marks)
subQuestions.memoText:
Award marks for well-explained strategies (1 mark for strategy + 1 mark for explanation/how it reduces UHI, up to 8 marks):

• Increase urban green spaces/parks and urban forests → trees and grass provide shade and release moisture through evapotranspiration, cooling the air. (2)
• Green/vegetated rooftops (rooftop gardens) → reduce heat absorption by roofs; plants cool through evapotranspiration. (2)
• Use light-coloured/reflective surfaces on buildings and roads (cool pavements/cool roofs) → reflect more solar radiation, absorbing less heat. (2)
• Plant street trees along roads → shade reduces surface temperatures and solar heating of roads. (2)
• Reduce car use / promote public transport → less waste heat from vehicle engines and less CO₂/pollution. (2)
• Use permeable/porous paving materials → allow water infiltration and evaporative cooling. (2)
• Install water features (fountains, ponds) → evaporation cools surrounding air. (2)
• Build with energy-efficient designs (passive cooling, better insulation) → less air conditioning waste heat released. (2)
• Urban planning that maintains open spaces and green corridors → allows cool rural air to penetrate urban areas. (2)

Note: Award max 8 marks. Full marks require at least 4 well-explained strategies with both the strategy and the mechanism by which it reduces the UHI effect.

subQuestions.questionText: The process whereby a river removes material from its bed and banks is called … (A: deposition / B: transportation / C: abrasion / D: erosion)
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D (erosion) (1 mark)
Erosion is the process by which a river removes/wears away material from its bed and banks through hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition, and solution.

subQuestions.questionText: Which ONE of the following is a feature of a youthful river? (A: Wide floodplain / B: Meanders / C: V-shaped valley / D: Oxbow lake)
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: A (V-shaped valley)

Wait — the memo answer for 2.1.2 is A: V-shaped valley.

Correct answer: A (V-shaped valley) (1 mark)
A youthful/upper course river is characterised by a V-shaped valley, steep gradient, fast flow, and dominance of vertical erosion. Meanders and oxbow lakes are features of the mature/old stage.

subQuestions.questionText: The load carried by a river suspended in the water is called the … (A: bed load / B: saltation load / C: suspended load / D: solution load)
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C (suspended load) (1 mark)
The suspended load consists of fine particles of silt and clay that are carried within the body of water without touching the riverbed. It gives rivers their characteristic muddy/brown appearance.

subQuestions.questionText: Graded rivers are characterised by … (A: maximum erosion throughout the channel / B: a balance between erosion and deposition / C: maximum deposition throughout the channel / D: increased velocity towards the source)
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B (a balance between erosion and deposition) (1 mark)
A graded river is in a state of dynamic equilibrium (grade) where the energy of the river is just sufficient to transport its load — erosion and deposition are balanced and there is no net change in the channel.

options.B: a balance between erosion and deposition

subQuestions.questionText: River rejuvenation occurs when … (A: the river loses energy and deposits material / B: there is a relative fall in base level / C: the river reaches a state of grade / D: sea levels rise relative to the land)
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C (there is a relative fall in base level)

Actually the standard answer is B: there is a relative fall in base level.

Correct answer: B (there is a relative fall in base level) (1 mark)
River rejuvenation is triggered by a relative fall in base level (the level to which a river erodes, usually sea level). This can result from tectonic uplift of the land or a fall in sea level, giving the river renewed erosive energy.

options.A: the river loses energy and deposits material
options.B: there is a relative fall in base level
options.C: the river reaches a state of grade
options.D: sea levels rise relative to the land

subQuestions.questionText: A knickpoint is a feature associated with … (A: river rejuvenation / B: river deposition / C: river grading / D: river drainage patterns)
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: A (river rejuvenation) (1 mark)
A knickpoint (also spelled nickpoint) is a break or irregularity in the long profile of a river, typically a waterfall or rapid, that forms where a rejuvenated river is actively cutting downwards and the new profile meets the old profile.

subQuestions.questionText: Incised meanders are formed when … (A: a river deposits material on the inside bend of a meander / B: a mature river is rejuvenated and vertical erosion deepens the meander / C: a river meanders across a flat floodplain / D: a river cuts off a meander loop to form an oxbow lake)
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D (a mature river is rejuvenated and vertical erosion deepens the meander)

Correct answer: B (a mature river is rejuvenated and vertical erosion deepens the meander) (1 mark)
Incised/entrenched meanders form when a meandering river is rejuvenated — the sudden increase in erosive energy causes the river to cut vertically downwards into its bed, preserving the meandering pattern but deepening the valley.

options.A: a river deposits material on the inside bend of a meander
options.B: a mature river is rejuvenated and vertical erosion deepens the meander
options.C: a river meanders across a flat floodplain
options.D: a river cuts off a meander loop to form an oxbow lake

subQuestions.questionText: Which ONE of the following is a human intervention used in river management? (A: Natural levée formation / B: Meander development / C: Dam construction / D: Floodplain formation)
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: A (Dam construction)

Correct answer: C (Dam construction) (1 mark)
Dam construction is a major human intervention in river management, used to control flooding, store water for irrigation and domestic use, and generate hydroelectric power. Natural levées, meanders, and floodplains are natural features.

subQuestions.questionText:
Match each drainage basin term in COLUMN A with the correct description in COLUMN B. Write only the letter (A–G) next to the question number.
2.2.1: Watershed
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D (1 mark)
A watershed (also called a drainage divide) is the boundary/highland area that separates one drainage basin from another, directing precipitation into different river systems.

subQuestions.questionText:
Match each drainage basin term in COLUMN A with the correct description in COLUMN B.
2.2.2: Tributary
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C (1 mark)
A tributary is a smaller stream or river that flows into and joins a larger river (the main stream/trunk stream).

subQuestions.questionText:
Match each drainage basin term in COLUMN A with the correct description in COLUMN B.
2.2.3: Confluence
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: E (1 mark)
A confluence is the point where two or more rivers/streams meet and join together.

subQuestions.questionText:
Match each drainage basin term in COLUMN A with the correct description in COLUMN B.
2.2.4: Drainage basin
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: F or A (accept either) (1 mark)
A drainage basin is the total land area drained by a river and all its tributaries. All precipitation falling within this area eventually flows into the main river.

subQuestions.questionText:
Match each drainage basin term in COLUMN A with the correct description in COLUMN B.
2.2.5: Source
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B (1 mark)
The source is the origin/starting point of a river, usually found in highland/mountainous areas where precipitation accumulates or where springs emerge.

subQuestions.questionText:
Match each drainage basin term in COLUMN A with the correct description in COLUMN B.
2.2.6: Mouth
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: G (1 mark)
The mouth of a river is where the river ends — the point where it flows into a larger body of water such as the sea, a lake, or another river.

subQuestions.questionText:
Match each drainage basin term in COLUMN A with the correct description in COLUMN B.
2.2.7: Interfluve
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: A (1 mark)
An interfluve is the area of higher ground between two adjacent river valleys or drainage basins. It forms the ridge or upland area separating two river systems.

subQuestions.questionText: Study the diagram showing a long profile/graded river. Define the term 'long profile of a river'.
subQuestions.memoText:
The long profile of a river is a cross-section/diagram showing the gradient/slope of a river (1) from its source to its mouth (1).

It illustrates how the gradient changes along the course of the river — typically steepest at the source and gentlest near the mouth — forming a concave curve in a graded river.

subQuestions.questionText: Explain why the long profile of a graded river is concave.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award up to 2 marks:
• Near the source, the river has a steep gradient (1) and high velocity, which allows it to erode its bed rapidly, creating a steep section.
• As the river flows towards the mouth, the gradient decreases (1) because the river has deposited its coarser material and the channel widens and deepens.
• The overall shape is concave because erosion is greatest in the upper course (steep) and deposition dominates in the lower course (gentle gradient), producing a smooth, curved profile. (2 marks for full explanation)
• The river adjusts its gradient through erosion and deposition to achieve grade — the concave shape represents the equilibrium profile.

subQuestions.questionText: Identify the base level of a river on the diagram.
subQuestions.memoText:
Sea level / the ocean / the lake (into which the river flows) (1 mark)
Base level is the lowest level to which a river can erode. The ultimate base level is sea level, though temporary base levels can be created by resistant rock, lakes, or dams along the river course.

subQuestions.questionText: Explain how changes in the base level can affect a river's long profile.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award up to 2 marks:
• If base level falls (e.g. sea level drops or land uplifts), the river has more vertical distance to erode, so it cuts downwards more aggressively — this is rejuvenation. (1)
• A new graded profile develops below the old one, separated by a knickpoint. (1)
• If base level rises (e.g. sea level rises), the river loses energy and deposits material, building up its channel. (1)
• The river adjusts its long profile to reach a new state of grade in response to the base level change. (1)
(Max 2 marks)

subQuestions.questionText: Explain the difference between a graded and an ungraded river.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award up to 2 marks:
• A graded river has achieved a state of dynamic equilibrium (1) where the energy of the river is just sufficient to transport its load — there is a balance between erosion and deposition and no net change in the channel. (1)
• An ungraded river has not achieved this balance (1) — it either has excess energy (eroding its bed) or insufficient energy (depositing load), and is still adjusting its long profile. (1)
(Max 2 marks)

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss the factors that influence the gradient of a river. (6 marks)
subQuestions.memoText:
Award marks for well-explained factors (1 mark for factor + 1 mark for explanation, up to 6 marks):

• Rock type/geology: Resistant/hard rocks slow down erosion, maintaining steeper gradients; softer rocks erode more easily, flattening the gradient. (2)
• Distance from source: Gradient is steepest at the source and decreases progressively towards the mouth as the river loses energy. (2)
• Discharge/volume of water: Higher discharge increases river energy and erosive power, helping the river cut downwards more effectively. (2)
• Tectonic activity: Uplift of land increases the gradient by raising the land relative to base level; subsidence reduces gradient. (2)
• Base level changes: A fall in base level (rejuvenation) steepens the gradient as the river cuts downwards; a rise in base level reduces gradient. (2)
• Human interference: Dams create new temporary base levels, reducing gradient upstream of the dam and potentially increasing it below. (2)
• Tributary input: Large tributaries increase discharge, which can increase erosion and affect gradient. (1)

Note: Full marks (6) require at least three well-explained factors with both identification and effect on gradient.

subQuestions.questionText: Study the diagram showing river rejuvenation features. Define the term 'river rejuvenation'.
subQuestions.memoText:
River rejuvenation is the process whereby a river gains renewed/increased erosive energy (1) as a result of a relative fall in base level (e.g. a fall in sea level or an uplift of the land) (1).

This causes the river to begin cutting downwards again (vertical/downward erosion), even if it had previously reached a state of grade.

subQuestions.questionText: Identify ONE feature of river rejuvenation shown in the diagram.
subQuestions.memoText:
Accept any ONE of the following (1 mark):
• Knickpoint / waterfall / rapids
• Incised/entrenched meanders
• River terraces
• Rejuvenated valley (V-shaped valley within a broader older valley)

subQuestions.questionText: Explain the formation of river terraces.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award up to 2 marks:
• River terraces form when a river is rejuvenated and begins to cut downwards (vertical erosion) into its own floodplain (1).
• The former floodplain is left as flat, elevated 'steps' or terraces on either side of the new, deeper channel (1).
• Multiple episodes of rejuvenation can create multiple levels of terraces (paired terraces) on either side of the valley.
• Each terrace represents a former floodplain level from a different period of river activity.

subQuestions.questionText: Explain the formation of a knickpoint.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award up to 2 marks:
• A knickpoint forms when a river is rejuvenated — the river begins to cut downwards from its new, lower base level (1).
• The point where the newly graded profile (below) meets the old profile (above) creates a sudden break in slope — a knickpoint — usually expressed as a waterfall or rapids (1).
• The knickpoint migrates upstream over time as the river continues to cut downwards and erodes the resistant rock at the break in slope.
• The knickpoint marks the upstream limit of rejuvenation at any given time.

subQuestions.questionText: Explain the formation of incised meanders.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Incised/entrenched meanders form when a mature, meandering river is rejuvenated (1).
• Rejuvenation occurs due to a relative fall in base level — either the land is uplifted tectonically or sea level falls (1).
• The river gains renewed vertical erosive energy and begins to cut downwards into its bed (1).
• Because the river was already meandering, the downward cutting follows the existing meander pattern, cutting the meander deeper into the landscape (1).
• The result is a deeply incised valley with a meandering course — the meanders are preserved but are now cut deeply into the bedrock rather than existing on a flat floodplain (1).
• The valley walls become steep and the river occupies the lowest part of the incised valley.
(Max 4 marks)

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss the causes of river rejuvenation. (4 marks)
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 1 mark per valid cause with explanation, up to 4 marks:

• Eustatic sea level change: A worldwide/global fall in sea level (e.g. during ice ages when water is locked in ice sheets) lowers the base level relative to the land, causing rivers to cut downwards. (2)
• Isostatic uplift: The land rises (e.g. after ice melts and the weight on the crust is removed — post-glacial rebound), effectively lowering the base level relative to the land surface, triggering downcutting. (2)
• Tectonic activity: Tectonic forces uplift the land surface, increasing the gradient and giving the river renewed erosive energy. (2)
• Epeirogenic movements: Large-scale, slow vertical movements of the Earth's crust can raise land above sea level, initiating rejuvenation. (2)
• Relative fall in local base level: Resistance of rock removed (e.g. a lake drained), lowering a temporary base level and allowing renewed downcutting. (1)
(Max 4 marks — award 1 mark for identifying the cause and 1 for explaining how it causes rejuvenation)

subQuestions.questionText: Study the diagram/image related to river management. Define the term 'river management'.
subQuestions.memoText:
River management refers to the human control and modification of rivers (1) to minimise the negative effects of flooding and to maximise the beneficial use of water resources for human needs (1).

It involves engineering works, conservation practices, and integrated water resource management strategies.

subQuestions.questionText: Identify ONE negative environmental impact of dam construction.
subQuestions.memoText:
Accept any ONE of the following (1 mark):
• Disruption/blocking of fish migration routes (e.g. fish cannot reach spawning grounds).
• Alteration of sediment flow downstream — reduced sediment leads to erosion of riverbeds and deltas below the dam.
• Flooding of natural habitats and ecosystems upstream (reservoir creation destroys existing ecosystems).
• Changes in water temperature and oxygen levels affecting aquatic life downstream.
• Displacement of human settlements and wildlife due to reservoir flooding.
• Increased risk of earthquakes due to the weight of water in the reservoir (reservoir-induced seismicity).

subQuestions.questionText: Explain how channelisation is used as a river management strategy.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award up to 2 marks:
• Channelisation involves straightening, widening, deepening, or lining a river channel with concrete or rock (1).
• This increases the velocity and efficiency of water flow, allowing more water to pass through the channel more quickly (1), thereby reducing the risk of flooding upstream.
• It may also involve removing obstacles, dredging sediment, and cutting off meanders to create a shorter, straighter channel.
• While effective at moving water quickly, channelisation can increase flood risk downstream and damage aquatic habitats.

subQuestions.questionText: Explain the role of afforestation in managing river flooding.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award up to 2 marks:
• Afforestation (planting trees in a catchment area) intercepts rainfall — leaves and branches catch rain before it reaches the ground, reducing surface runoff (1).
• Tree roots increase soil infiltration capacity, allowing more water to soak into the ground rather than running into rivers (1).
• This reduces the amount of water reaching rivers quickly after rainfall events, lowering peak discharge and reducing flood risk.
• Vegetation also stabilises soil and reduces erosion, decreasing the sediment load in rivers.

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using dams as a river management strategy. (8 marks)
subQuestions.memoText:
Award marks for well-explained advantages and disadvantages (1 mark for point + 1 mark for elaboration/consequence, up to 8 marks). Full marks require a balance of advantages and disadvantages.

ADVANTAGES:
• Flood control: Dams regulate water flow and can store excess water during floods, releasing it gradually to prevent downstream flooding. (2)
• Water storage/supply: Reservoirs store water for domestic, industrial, and agricultural use, ensuring a reliable water supply in dry periods. (2)
• Hydroelectric power generation: Dams can be used to generate clean, renewable electricity (HEP), reducing dependence on fossil fuels. (2)
• Irrigation: Stored water can be released for irrigation, enabling agriculture in areas that would otherwise be too dry. (2)
• Recreation: Reservoirs provide opportunities for water sports, tourism, and fishing, boosting local economies. (1)

DISADVANTAGES:
• Environmental disruption: Dams block fish migration and alter downstream ecosystems through reduced sediment flow and changed water temperatures. (2)
• Displacement of communities: Construction of reservoirs floods inhabited areas, forcing people to relocate. (2)
• High cost: Construction and maintenance of dams is extremely expensive. (1)
• Siltation: Sediment accumulates in the reservoir over time, reducing storage capacity and the dam's lifespan. (2)
• Downstream erosion: Reduced sediment load below the dam causes erosion of riverbeds, banks, and deltas. (2)
• Risk of dam failure: Structural failure of a dam can cause catastrophic flooding downstream. (1)

Note: Maximum 8 marks. Award marks proportionally for advantages and disadvantages. A one-sided answer cannot receive full marks.
